name: Afro-Asiatic Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Afro-Asiatic languages have a masculine/feminine gender distinction that triggers agreement on verbs, adjectives, pronouns, and (in Semitic) numerals. Some Cushitic and Omotic languages have more complex gender/class systems. Gender assignment is partly semantic, partly arbitrary.

linguisticChallenges.rootBasedMorphology: Semitic branch languages use a root-and-pattern (templatic) morphological system where consonantal roots (typically 3 consonants) are combined with vowel patterns and affixes to derive meaning. This is fundamentally different from concatenative morphology and requires understanding of abstract root extraction. Other branches (Berber, Cushitic, Chadic) show varying degrees of this system.
linguisticChallenges.morphologicalComplexity: Afro-Asiatic languages span a wide range of morphological complexity — from extensive templatic morphology (Arabic, Hebrew) to more analytic structures (some Chadic languages). Verbal morphology is generally rich, encoding subject, sometimes object, tense, aspect, and mood.
linguisticChallenges.genderAgreement: The masculine/feminine gender system triggers agreement chains across clauses. Number and gender interact in complex ways — e.g., Arabic numerals show reverse gender agreement (feminine numeral with masculine noun and vice versa).
linguisticChallenges.pluralFormation: Plural formation is highly irregular across the family. Semitic languages famously use 'broken plurals' (internal vowel changes) alongside 'sound plurals' (suffixation), with no reliable rule for predicting which pattern a noun takes.
linguisticChallenges.wordOrderVariation: Word order varies significantly: VSO (Classical Arabic, Hebrew), SVO (many modern varieties), SOV (some Cushitic, Omotic). Genus-level cards specify word order for each branch.

notes: Family card for Afro-Asiatic (~380 members). Covers Semitic (Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic), Berber, Cushitic (Somali, Oromo), Chadic (Hausa), Omotic, and Egyptian. The genus-semitic.json card provides Semitic-specific properties. Script and direction are null because the family includes both RTL (Arabic, Hebrew) and LTR (Amharic/Ge'ez, Latin for Hausa/Berber) scripts.
